title: The Poisoned Meal at Khaybar
subtitle: The Treacherous Offering, the Martyrdom of Bishr, and the Rigorous Hadith Tradition
summary: Following the conclusion of hostilies at Khaybar, a roasted sheep laced with lethal poison was presented to the Prophet by a local woman seeking vengeance. The incident, recorded in authentic Hadith collections, resulted in the immediate martyrdom of Bishr ibn al-Bara' and left enduring physical effects upon the Prophet until his final illness. Classical scholarship rigorously analyzes the theological, legal, and historical dimensions of the episode while avoiding sensationalism.

sections.text: In the days following the capitulation of the fortresses, as the terms of the agricultural settlement were being finalized, an incident occurred that revealed the lingering hostility harbored by certain factions of Khaybar's vanquished aristocracy. Zaynab bint al-Harith, the wife of Sallam ibn Mishkam—a prominent Jewish leader who had fallen during the siege—conceived a plot to assassinate the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. Knowing that the Prophet accepted gifts of food but never consumed charity, she inquired of his companions which portion of a roasted sheep he preferred most. Upon learning that he favored the shoulder, she prepared a roasted lamb, saturating the shoulder and the entire carcass with a potent and fast-acting poison.

Zaynab brought the roasted sheep to the Prophet's quarters, presenting it as an act of hospitality and reconciliation. Accompanying the Prophet was his loyal companion Bishr ibn al-Bara' ibn Ma'rur. Welcoming the gift in accordance with his customary graciousness, the Prophet took a morsel from the shoulder and chewed it, while Bishr took a piece from another section and swallowed it immediately.
Before swallowing the morsel, the Prophet spat it out upon his hand, recognizing instantly that the meat was tainted. He turned immediately to his companions and commanded with urgency:

ارْفَعُوا أَيْدِيَكُمْ، فَإِنَّهَا أَخْبَرَتْنِي أَنَّهَا مَسْمُومَةٌ
'Lift your hands! For this bone informs me that it has been poisoned.' (Sahih al-Bukhari 2617, 3169; Sahih Muslim 2190; Sunan Abi Dawud 4510)

Tragically, the poison was so lethal and concentrated that Bishr ibn al-Bara', having swallowed his morsel, rapidly succumbed to its toxicity. Authentic reports record that his skin changed color and he passed away shortly thereafter, attaining martyrdom in the path of Allah.

The woman was immediately summoned and brought before the Messenger of Allah ﷺ for questioning. When confronted, she confessed without denial, explaining the motive behind her calculated treason: 'You know what you have done to my father, my uncle, and my husband. I said to myself: If he is merely a king and a worldly conqueror, we will be rid of him; and if he is truly a prophet of God, he will be miraculously informed and the poison will not harm him.'

The companions, furious at the treacherous attempt on the Prophet's life and the tragic death of Bishr, asked: 'Shall we kill her, O Messenger of Allah?' According to the narration in Sahih al-Bukhari, the Prophet initially declined to execute her for the personal grievance against himself, manifesting his extraordinary capacity for personal forbearance. However, classical jurists document that once Bishr ibn al-Bara' succumbed to the fatal effects of the poison, she was subsequently subjected to legal retribution (qisas) at the request of Bishr's heirs to satisfy the demands of justice for murder.
Long-Term Medical Effects and Theological Reflection

Although the Prophet spat out the poisoned flesh, a small trace of the toxic substance had absorbed into his system. For the remaining four years of his life, the Prophet occasionally experienced recurring pain from that incident during seasonal changes. In an authentic narration in Sahih al-Bukhari, the Mother of the Believers Aisha narrated that during his final illness, the Prophet said to her: 'O Aisha, I continue to feel the pain of the morsel I ate at Khaybar, and this is the time when my aorta feels severed from that poison.'

Classical scholars such as Ibn Hajar al-Asqalani and Ibn Kathir reflect upon this narration with deep theological insight. They observe that Allah protected His Messenger from dying immediately at Khaybar, ensuring that his prophetic mission would reach complete perfection and historical culmination, while ultimately granting him the supreme station of martyrdom through the lingering effects of the sacrifice endured in His cause.
